newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa considering arms sales to Syria -- official.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa considering arms sales to Syria -- official.

text.p: South Africa is considering selling weapons systems worth three billion rand ($641 million) to Syria, officials said on Sunday.

Johannesburg's Sunday Times said the cabinet had given conditional approval for the supply of tank firing systems to the Damascus government, which is listed by the United States as a "state sponsor of terrorism".

The cabinet, fearing the move could anger Washington, "made its support conditional on the approval of Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, who was not at the meeting at which the issue was discussed", the newspaper said.
Mbeki was studying the matter and was expected to decide by the first cabinet meeting of the new year on January 22, his spokesman told Reuters.
"He will have studied the matter by then and will raise it and hopefully a decision would be made at that time," Ricky Naidoo said.
A source close to the state weapons agency said the equipment in question was an electronic system for computerised control of the mechanism which fires the cannon in tanks and howitzers.
The newspaper reports said there had been debate among arms control officials as to whether or not the system fell within the U.S. definition of lethal military equipment.
A spokesman for President Nelson Mandela was unable to say if he had been consulted on the proposed sale.
Cabinet secretary Jakes Gerwel said the issue had come up in December.
"It involves quite a lot of consultation, most of which could not take place because of the time of the year," Johannesburg's Sunday Independent quoted him as saying.
December and January is the peak summer holiday season in South Africa, when most industries shut down and parliament closes.
South Africa's former white government built up a formidable arms industry during its decades of isolation under apartheid.
Although it was a close ally of Israel, it sold weapons to both sides in the Iran-Iraq war during the 1980s and arms from Pretoria also reached Lebanon.

But President Nelson Mandela's government, brought to power in the country's first all-race elections in 1994, has so far avoided sales to the troubled Middle East under a policy of not supplying weapons to countries that threaten their neighbours.
Mandela's government has come under fire several times from the United States for its links to Libya, Iran and Cuba.
Defence Minister Joe Modise announced in November that South Africa had sold weapons worth nearly one billion rand ($214 million) to 62 countries in the year to September 30.
